project_type: Internal payment-operations web application (B2B internal tool, financial)
project_description: Internal tool for Insurance Revolution staff to create Worldpay hosted-payment links, send them to customers by email and SMS, and track payment and communication status. Single Next.js 12 application with frontend and API routes in one codebase, MySQL via Prisma, deployed as a Docker container to Azure App Service.

audit.subject: Abraham Akintola (AbrahamNobleOX)
audit.production_database_note: Live production database (Azure Database for MySQL 8.0.46, database 'appdb') accessed read-only on 2026-10-10 via a connection string held commented-out in .env. Session ran SET SESSION TRANSACTION READ ONLY with server confirmation @@transaction_read_only=1, so MySQL itself would reject any write. Guard script additionally refused all write/DDL keywords. Only SELECT, aggregate and SHOW statements executed. No schema, data or configuration modified.
audit.database_access_method: TLS connection (--ssl-mode=REQUIRED). Read-only transaction mode, server-verified. Bounded aggregates and GROUP BY rollups only; no bulk raw-row extraction. A local Docker development database was also started, queried under the same guard, and returned to its stopped state.
audit.pii_and_secrets: No credentials, connection strings, tokens or keys recorded. Only environment variable names read. No customer PII reproduced; all database findings are aggregate counts.

dates.production_golive_evidence: 2026 Prisma migrations applied to production 2026-07-17 18:26; first AuthUser and AuditLog rows 19:33 same evening.

engineering_challenges.challenge: Retrofitting authorisation into a live authenticated application
engineering_challenges.why_hard: Inserting enforcement without locking out existing users mid-rollout. Solved with a bootstrap admin from configuration and three independent environment flags allowing domain checks and invite requirements to be tightened separately at runtime.

engineering_challenges.challenge: Bulk operations over a payment provider with partial failure
engineering_challenges.why_hard: Each item makes up to three external calls across two channels, any of which can fail independently. Required separate link/email/SMS state per item, aggregated job counters, and a distinct completed_with_errors terminal state so operators can see precisely which recipients failed and why.

engineering_challenges.challenge: Signing correctness with a legacy hosted-payment integration
engineering_challenges.why_hard: Hosted-page parameters are client-visible and alterable, so an unsigned link allows amount tampering. The signature must cover exactly the configured fields in order; a partially-populated set would produce a valid signature over the wrong data.
No App Router, route handlers or built-in job support. Required an in-process deferred execution pattern plus durable job tables, with explicitly understood limits.
Script had to be re-runnable, incremental and verifiable before committing - hence upsert-by-uuid, --since, batching and --dry-run.

decisions.decision: Application-owned authorisation rather than Google Workspace groups
decisions.problem: Needed roles, invites and disablement tied to app-specific permissions.
decisions.reasoning: Permissions are domain-specific (payments.export, payments.send) and map poorly onto directory groups; keeps the audit trail adjacent to the payment data it describes.
decisions.tradeoffs: A second user store to maintain; offboarding is not automatic when a Google account is disabled.
decisions.result: Granular per-route enforcement; auth.denied events confirm the path is exercised.

decisions.decision: In-process asynchronous job execution rather than a queue or worker service
decisions.problem: Bulk resend involves many external calls and cannot run inside a request.
decisions.reasoning: Avoids introducing a broker and separate worker deployment for a single internal workflow on one App Service.
decisions.tradeoffs: Duplicate-run guard is per-process so would not prevent concurrency across instances; instance restart mid-job leaves items pending with no automatic resumption.
decisions.result: Working bulk processing with no new infrastructure; durable item state leaves a clean upgrade path to a real queue.

decisions.decision: Database-backed sender configuration rather than environment variables
decisions.problem: UCP sender addresses change and must match senders pre-approved in UCP.
decisions.reasoning: Changing a sender should not require a redeploy.
decisions.tradeoffs: Configuration split between env vars and database.
decisions.result: Misconfiguration surfaces as an explicit actionable error rather than silent delivery failure.

decisions.decision: Resolve production connection string from Azure at deploy time
decisions.reasoning: Avoids duplicating the production connection string into GitHub secrets; single source of truth.
decisions.tradeoffs: Pipeline needs a service principal with configuration read rights.
decisions.result: No database credentials in the repository or CI - corroborated by this audit finding only local strings in .env.

decisions.decision: Keep Next.js 12 pages router rather than upgrading
decisions.problem: Framework was several major versions behind.
decisions.reasoning: Goal was security and operational capability, not framework migration; an upgrade would have risked the live payment flow.
decisions.tradeoffs: No App Router features; legacy next/link semantics.
decisions.result: Substantial capability added with the core payment path untouched.

problems_solved.problem: Payment links expiring unnoticed with no bulk remediation
problems_solved.solution: Added link_expires_at with dedicated index, derived a four-state link status, exposed it as a dashboard filter, and built bulk resend with optional regeneration.

problems_solved.problem: Silent delivery failures after the UCP migration
problems_solved.solution: Typed MissingUcpSenderConfigError with remediation text naming the admin screen, surfaced to the operator instead of logged and swallowed.

problems_solved.problem: Unsigned payment links allowing amount tampering
problems_solved.solution: MD5 signing over configured fields, refusal to sign on missing fields, fail-closed on absent configuration, independent amount verification in the callback.
problems_solved.evidence: payment/new.ts; public/payment/response.ts; documented as non-removable in AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md

problems_solved.solution: Identified plain anchor tags bypassing the Next.js router; converted navigation, table row links and menu items to next/link. Rejected a React Router proposal as incompatible with the pages router and unnecessary.

problems_solved.problem: Validation errors arriving as HTTP 400s with no client-side guard
problems_solved.solution: Added client-side yup schemas mirroring server rules plus a mergeFieldErrors helper, while retaining server validation as authoritative for all callers.

lessons: Undocumented legacy integrations are a research problem before they are a coding problem - the signing fix was ~40 lines, but nearly all the risk sat in establishing which fields the installation verified and in what order, with a failure mode that can look like success. Failing closed and refusing partial signatures were the safeguards against being wrong.
Fixing the real problem earns the mandate for the rest - the engagement began as one security fix and expanded into access control, auditing, reporting and bulk remediation.
Retrofitting access control is a migration problem, not a modelling problem - the valuable design work was the bootstrap admin and independent feature flags, not the permission table.
Model partial failure explicitly when fanning out to external providers; per-channel state turns an opaque failure into an actionable one.
Fail closed and say why - typed errors with remediation text converted silent misconfiguration into visible, fixable messages.
Configuration belongs where its change cadence lives: secrets in environment variables, operationally-tuned values in the database behind an admin screen.
An in-process job runner is a legitimate interim choice only if the state is durable; persisting job items made the shortcut defensible and kept a queue migration cheap.
Would do differently: automated tests on signing, permission middleware and bulk-resend state transitions; retry with backoff on provider calls; job resumption after restart.

interview_stories.title: The payment links customers could rewrite
interview_stories.situation: Brought into a four-year-old internal payment platform for one reason: customers were paying less than they were invoiced. The amount travelled in the Worldpay hosted-page URL as a plain query parameter, so a link for £500 could be edited to £5.
interview_stories.task: Close it in a live financial system without breaking the daily payment flow.
interview_stories.action: Traced the full failure path first - a 2022 callback check rejected mismatched amounts, so money was taken at the provider but never recorded, surfacing as an accounting mess rather than clean underpayment. Implemented MD5 signing with a configuration-driven ordered field list, a throw-on-missing-field guard so a partial parameter set can never be signed, fail-closed behaviour when signing config is absent, and deliberate retention of the existing callback check as an independent second layer.
interview_stories.result: Shipped as the first substantive commit ~10 days after joining; closed an exposure surface of 65,093 links worth £45M; previous developers had reportedly failed at it; CTO commended the fix; the engagement then expanded into the wider modernisation.
interview_stories.evidence: Pre-fix source has no signature; git blame attributes all 36 signing lines to the 2026-07-05 commit; production data sizes the exposure.
interview_stories.what_id_do_differently: Write tests around the signing logic - still the highest-risk untested code in the system.

interview_stories.title: Retrofitting access control into a live financial tool
interview_stories.situation: An internal tool generating customer payment links allowed any company Google account full access, with no audit trail.
interview_stories.task: Introduce roles, invites and disablement without locking out active users or disrupting payment operations.
interview_stories.action: Designed app-owned authorisation (3 roles, 7 permissions) with hashed single-use invite tokens and 48h TTL; permission middleware per route; bootstrap admin from configuration; domain enforcement and invite requirement behind independent environment flags.
interview_stories.result: Granular enforcement with a complete audit trail; auth.denied events confirm the rejection path is active.

interview_stories.title: Designing for partial failure in a bulk external fan-out
interview_stories.situation: Operators needed to resend hundreds of pending payment links at once.
interview_stories.task: Build bulk processing where each item makes up to three external calls across two channels, any of which can fail.
interview_stories.action: Modelled a parent job and per-item rows with independent link/email/SMS state; isolated failures per item; aggregated counters; distinguished completed from completed_with_errors; capped jobs at 5,000; guarded against duplicate concurrent runs.
interview_stories.result: Operators can see exactly which recipients failed and why instead of a single opaque failure.
interview_stories.evidence: bulk-payment-resend.service.ts; local run 2 jobs, 3/3 items sent

interview_stories.title: A deliberate shortcut, and knowing its limits
interview_stories.situation: Bulk jobs needed background execution; stack was Next.js 12 on a single App Service with no queue infrastructure.
interview_stories.action: Chose durable job/item tables plus in-process deferred execution with a duplicate-run guard rather than introducing a broker and worker deployment.
interview_stories.result: Delivered the capability with no new infrastructure.
interview_stories.reflection: The guard is per-process and would not hold across instances; a restart mid-job leaves items pending with no automatic resumption. Durable item state was the deliberate hedge keeping a queue migration cheap.

interview_stories.title: Debugging full-page reloads
interview_stories.situation: Every navigation reloaded the entire application; a proposal to adopt React Router was on the table.
interview_stories.action: Identified that several links were plain anchors bypassing the Next.js router, and that React Router is incompatible with the pages router; converted navigation, table row links and menu items to next/link.
interview_stories.result: Client-side transitions with prefetching; the correct fix was a handful of components, not a routing library.

interview_stories.title: Reading a 400 correctly before fixing it
interview_stories.situation: Submitting an empty form produced 400 Bad Request errors in the console.
interview_stories.action: Traced the flow and established the 400 was the validation mechanism; added mirrored client-side validation for instant feedback while deliberately retaining server validation as authoritative for all API callers.
interview_stories.result: Immediate feedback; 400s reserved for genuine anomalies; no weakening of the security boundary.

interview_stories.title: Securing a legacy hosted-payment integration
interview_stories.situation: Worldpay hosted pages carry the amount in a client-visible URL.
interview_stories.action: MD5 signing over configured fields; refusal to sign when any field is missing; fail-closed when signing configuration is absent; independent amount re-verification in the callback.
interview_stories.result: Defence in depth on the financially sensitive field.

audit_limitations: Message volume counts application-logged send attempts, not provider-confirmed deliveries - the most significant remaining caveat.
The 68,869-record estate and its £34.95M paid value largely predate this contribution; only post-2026-07-17 figures are attributable, and the two must never be conflated.
git blame measures surviving lines at HEAD and favours the most recent contributor; reported alongside raw commit and diff counts.
Business motivations are inferred from code and documentation; no requirements or ticket records were available.
Deployment definitions and their database effects were verified, but GitHub Actions run history and Azure platform metrics were not accessible.
The repository's three .test.ts files are empty placeholders; no test suite was available to assess quality.

The post-release window (~3 months) is too short to assess any effect on payment conversion; no causal claim is made in either direction, and the lifetime average is not a valid baseline for that comparison.
development_environment_note: A local development database (14 payments, 2 users) was also inspected but is NOT cited as evidence; all metrics above come from production.

engagement_origin.summary: Brought onto the project specifically to fix a parameter-tampering vulnerability in the Worldpay payment links that allowed customers to alter the amount they paid.

vulnerability.type: Parameter tampering / unsigned request in a hosted payment page integration
vulnerability.mechanism: getPaymentLink built the Worldpay URL as a plain query string including amount, with no signature of any kind. A recipient could rewrite &amount=500 to &amount=5 and complete a genuine checkout at the lower amount.
vulnerability.why_worse_than_underpayment: A pre-existing callback check (ef1ff7f, Michal Tesar, 2022-12-23) compared the amount reported by Worldpay against the stored amount and refused to mark mismatched payments as paid. The payment therefore completed at the provider - the card was charged - but was never recorded by the application, leaving unreconcilable receipts and permanently pending requests.
business_consequences: Accounting and reconciliation problems from payments taken but never recorded
Loss of customer trust in the payment links
Compounded by generic, unbranded payment emails that recipients found untrustworthy
vulnerability.evidence_level: VERIFIED (pre-fix source at af467f9^ shows no signature; callback check authorship confirmed by git log)

fix.significance: First substantive commit on the project, roughly ten days after joining (first activity 2026-06-25).
implementation: MD5 digest over a configurable, ordered field list (WP_SIGNATURE_FIELDS, default instId:amount:currency:cartId) joined with the shared secret, so the app can be aligned to the Worldpay installation without a code change
Throws if any signature field is missing or empty rather than signing a partial parameter set - a missing amount would otherwise produce a valid signature over the wrong data
assertWorldpayMd5Config() makes the system fail closed: no signing configuration means no link generation, surfaced as a validation-shaped error
Pre-existing callback amount check deliberately retained as an independent second layer (defence in depth)
fix.authorship: All 36 lines of the signing implementation attributed to af467f9 (AbrahamNobleOX) by git blame

difficulty.no_documentation: No surviving documentation for the legacy Worldpay integration. The hard part was determining which fields the installation verified and in what order - a failure mode that can silently appear to work while protecting nothing.
difficulty.prior_attempts: Other developers had reportedly attempted the fix without success.
difficulty.evidence_level: STRONGLY SUPPORTED (absence of docs consistent with repository state; prior attempts are the engineer's account, not independently verifiable)

recognition.action: Worth obtaining in writing - see evidence_gaps.

exposure_surface.calculation_method: COUNT(*) and SUM(amount) over Payment where created_at < '2026-07-05'
exposure_surface.critical_qualification: This is the EXPOSURE SURFACE - every link issued in the period carried an editable amount parameter. It is NOT a loss figure. Nothing establishes how many links were actually tampered with, because a tampered payment was rejected by the callback and left no record of the amount charged. Phrase as 'closed a vulnerability affecting £45M of issued payment links'; never 'saved' or 'prevented the loss of' £45M.

conversion_impact.reason: Only ~3 months of post-release data at time of audit; smallest difference distinguishable from normal variation was about +/-2 percentage points, so a modest effect could not be seen in either direction.
conversion_impact.do_not_claim: Do NOT use the lifetime-average comparison (post-release 78.9% vs lifetime 76.3%, apparent ~2.6pp gain). It is an artefact: the lifetime figure is depressed by a 2025 dip that had already recovered before the release (May and June 2026 both recorded 80.1%, higher than any later month). Make no conversion claim in either direction until re-measured.
conversion_impact.baseline_and_method: Held in the private working note 'Paid-rate baseline and re-check method.md' alongside this dossier - contains prepared pre/post figures, seasonal and size controls, maturity rule and statistical approach.
conversion_impact.note: The MD5 signing fix is justified as closing a security and accounting-integrity defect; its value does not depend on the conversion metric.
